stops.name: Paris, Green's Essay laid before Liouville and Sturm
stops.campa: Thomson shows the recovered pamphlet of George Green to Joseph Liouville and Charles-François Sturm, the leading mathematical physicists of Paris, and its unlooked-for depth causes something close to a sensation among men who had never heard the dead Englishman's name. Thomson arranges for the Essay to be reprinted in Crelle's Journal, the standard organ of continental mathematics, over the following years, so that a miller's son who taught himself potential theory in a Nottingham bakehouse is at last read where the mathematics of the age is actually made and judged.

stops.name: Glasgow, election to the Chair of Natural Philosophy
stops.campa: At twenty-two, fresh from Cambridge and Paris, William Thomson is elected Professor of Natural Philosophy at the University of Glasgow, the chair his own father has coached him for since boyhood. He will hold it for fifty-three years without a break, refusing repeated invitations to Cambridge, Oxford, and abroad. Colleagues expect a brilliant but conventional lecturer; instead the young professor immediately begins to drag the whole apparatus of experimental physics, batteries, coils, gauges, and eventually a teaching laboratory, into a curriculum that until now has been chalk and blackboard only.

stops.name: Glasgow, the founding of the first teaching laboratory
stops.campa: In a disused wine cellar under the old college, Thomson sets up what becomes recognized as the first undergraduate teaching laboratory of experimental physics in Britain, where students measure rather than merely watch. He buys instruments out of his own salary, badgers instrument-makers for improvements, and drills his classes in the same discipline of exact numbers he learned from Regnault in Paris. Decades later, students recall the cellar's damp and clutter with real affection: it is where natural philosophy in Scotland stops being a lecture and starts being a practice of the hands.

stops.name: Oxford, the meeting with James Prescott Joule
stops.campa: At the British Association meeting in Oxford, a young Manchester brewer named James Prescott Joule reads a paper claiming to have measured, with a paddle-wheel churning water in an insulated can, the exact mechanical equivalent of heat. Most of the assembled savants ignore it as amateur curiosity; Thomson alone rises from the audience to question Joule closely, half-convinced the brewer must be wrong, wholly unable to stop thinking about it afterward. He will spend the rest of the year unlearning the caloric theory of heat he was raised on, and starting the friendship that will remake thermodynamics.

stops.name: Chamonix, the waterfall experiment
stops.campa: By pure chance, walking in the valley of Chamonix that same summer, Thomson meets Joule again, thermometer in hand, on his honeymoon, still hunting for proof of his theory in the natural world. The two men climb together to a waterfall on the Sallanches road and attempt, half in earnest and half as a shared joke against the whole learned world, to measure whether water falling a great height arrives at the bottom warmer than it left the top, exactly as Joule's mechanical-equivalent theory predicts it must. The spray defeats the thermometer, but not the friendship, nor the theory.

stops.name: Glasgow, 'On an Absolute Thermometric Scale'
stops.campa: Working from Carnot's theory of the motive power of heat and from Regnault's Paris data on gases, Thomson publishes a scale of temperature that depends on no particular substance, water, mercury, or air, but on the theoretical behaviour of an ideal heat engine. He fixes its zero at the point where a gas's pressure would vanish altogether: minus 273 degrees on the old Celsius scale, a cold no vessel on Earth has ever reached but which the mathematics demands as an absolute floor beneath all possible temperature.
stops.quote: The characteristic property of the scale which I now propose is, that all degrees have the same value; that is, that a unit of heat descending from a body A at the temperature T° of this scale, to a body B at the temperature (T-1)°, would give out the same mechanical effect, whatever be the number T.
stops.quote_source: 'On an Absolute Thermometric Scale Founded on Carnot's Theory of the Motive Power of Heat', Philosophical Magazine (1848)

stops.name: Glasgow, 'On the Dynamical Theory of Heat'
stops.campa: Reading before the Royal Society of Edinburgh, Thomson lays out the dynamical theory of heat that reconciles Carnot's engine theory with Joule's mechanical equivalent, work he has been turning over since Oxford and Chamonix. In the same paper he states, independently of but consistent with Clausius on the Continent, the principle that will stand as the second law of thermodynamics: no engine, however perfect, can draw useful work from heat alone without some of that heat passing to a colder body. It becomes the axiom on which every steam engine, every refrigerator, and eventually every theory of the universe's slow decay will be built.
stops.quote: It is impossible, by means of inanimate material agency, to derive mechanical effect from any portion of matter by cooling it below the temperature of the coldest of the surrounding objects.
stops.quote_source: 'On the Dynamical Theory of Heat', Transactions of the Royal Society of Edinburgh (1851)

stops.name: Thornliebank, marriage to Margaret Crum
stops.campa: William marries Margaret Crum, daughter of the chemist and calico-printer Walter Crum of Thornliebank, a childhood friend of the family from summers on the Clyde. She is delicate in health from the start of the marriage, and will remain so for its whole eighteen years, following her husband on cable expeditions and instrument trials when she is well enough and waiting anxiously at Glasgow when she is not. Their household becomes, like his laboratory, an extension of the work: dinner-table talk of galvanometers and gutta-percha insulation, guests drawn from half the learned societies of Europe.

stops.name: Glasgow, appointment as director of the Atlantic Telegraph Company
stops.campa: Cyrus Field's newly formed Atlantic Telegraph Company enlists Thomson as one of its scientific directors, drawn by his 1855 theoretical paper proving that a signal sent down a long submarine cable spreads and slows in proportion to the square of the cable's length, the 'law of squares' that the company's own chief electrician, Wildman Whitehouse, publicly disputes and privately ignores. Thomson accepts unpaid, buys shares he can ill afford, and commits himself for the next decade to a wager that a wire two thousand four hundred miles long can be made to speak across an ocean floor no one has properly sounded.

stops.name: Mid-Atlantic, the cable snaps on the first expedition
stops.campa: Six days out from Valentia, with the Agamemnon and the Niagara paying out cable from opposite ends toward mid-ocean, a wave pitches the Niagara and a brake is clapped on too hard: the cable parts and two miles of copper and gutta-percha spool away to the sea floor, three hundred and eighty miles of the expedition's work lost in an instant. Thomson, aboard as scientific adviser, watches the whole apparatus of the enterprise, ships, money, reputation, sink with it. The company does not abandon the project; it orders more cable and books the ships again for the following summer.

stops.name: Glasgow, the invention of the mirror galvanometer
stops.campa: Over the winter following the failure, Thomson builds the instrument on which the whole project's second attempt will turn: a tiny mirror, no bigger than a shirt button, cemented to a magnetized needle and suspended within a coil, so that a beam of lamplight reflected off it swings across a graduated scale at the faintest current a submarine cable can carry. Where Whitehouse's crude receivers demand currents strong enough to burn the insulation, Thomson's mirror reads a signal too weak to feel. It is the instrument, more than any other single object, that will make transoceanic telegraphy possible.

stops.name: Mid-Atlantic, the mid-ocean splice
stops.campa: The Agamemnon and the Niagara meet at an agreed point in mid-Atlantic, splice their two cable-ends together, and turn away from each other, one steaming toward Valentia in Ireland, the other toward Trinity Bay in Newfoundland, paying out wire behind them at a steady four miles an hour. Thomson stands watch over the mirror galvanometer through storms that nearly founder the Agamemnon in the Bay of Biscay before the ships have even reached the splice point, reading the faint returning pulses that tell him, hour by hour, that the cable beneath them is still whole.
